claim: The majority of the genetic diversity on Earth is encoded by microbes.
source: The majority of the genetic diversity on Earth is encoded by microbes (Hug et al., 2016; Lapierre and Gogarten, 2009; Tara Oceans coordinators et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to three published studies (Hug et al., 2016; Lapierre and Gogarten, 2009; Tara Oceans coordinators et al., 2015)

claim: The functioning of all Earth's ecosystems is reliant on diverse microbial communities.
source: the functioning of all Earth's ecosystems is reliant on diverse microbial communities (Falkowski et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to Falkowski et al., 2008

claim: High-throughput 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing studies continue to yield unprecedented insight into the taxonomic richness of microbiomes.
source: High-throughput 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing studies continue to yield unprecedented insight into the taxonomic richness of microbiomes (e.g. Louca et al., 2019; Sogin et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citations to examples (Louca et al., 2019; Sogin et al., 2006)

claim: Abiotic drivers of community composition (e.g. pH) are increasingly characterized.
source: abiotic drivers of community composition (e.g. pH; Lauber et al., 2009; Power et al., 2018) are increasingly characterized
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on pH effects (Lauber et al., 2009; Power et al., 2018)

claim: Biotic (microbe-microbe) interactions can be important in determining community composition.
source: Although it is known that biotic (microbe-microbe) interactions can also be important in determining community composition (Needham and Fuhrman, 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to Needham and Fuhrman, 2016

claim: Comparatively little is known about how biotic interactions shape microbiome diversity as a whole.
source: comparatively little is known about how such interactions, either positive (e.g. cross-feeding; Seth and Taga, 2014) or negative (e.g. toxin-mediated interference competition; Czárán et al., 2002; Hibbing et al., 2010), shape microbiome diversity as a whole
evidence: Inference based on the state of the literature and citations to examples of positive and negative interactions

claim: Elton (1946) plotted the number of species versus the number of genera in 49 animal community samples and observed a ~ 1:1 ratio in each individual sample, but a ~ 4:1 ratio when all samples were pooled.
source: In an early study of 49 animal (vertebrate and invertebrate) community samples, Elton, 1946 plotted the number of species versus the number of genera and observed a ~ 1:1 ratio in each individual sample, but a ~ 4:1 ratio when all samples were pooled.
evidence: Supported by citation to Elton, 1946

claim: Elton took the observation of species:genus ratios as evidence for competitive exclusion preventing related species from co-existing.
source: He took this observation as evidence for competitive exclusion preventing related species, more likely to overlap in niche space, to co-exist.
evidence: Inference from Elton's work cited in the previous sentence

claim: Ecological Controls (EC) predicts speciation rates to decrease with increasing standing species diversity because less niche space is available.
source: This concept, more recently referred to as niche filling or Ecological Controls (EC) (Schluter and Pennell, 2017), predicts speciation (or, more generally, diversification) rates to decrease with increasing standing species diversity because less niche space is available (Rabosky and Hurlbert, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schluter and Pennell, 2017 and Rabosky and Hurlbert, 2015

claim: The Diversity Begets Diversity (DBD) model predicts that when species interactions create novel niches, standing biodiversity favours further diversification.
source: In contrast, the Diversity Begets Diversity (DBD) model predicts that when species interactions create novel niches, standing biodiversity favours further diversification (Calcagno et al., 2017; Whittaker, 1972).
evidence: Supported by citations to Calcagno et al., 2017 and Whittaker, 1972

claim: Niche construction could influence the evolution of the species constructing the niche, as well as that of co-occurring species.
source: For example, niche construction (i.e. the physical, chemical or biological alteration of the environment) could influence the evolution of the species constructing the niche, as well as that of co-occurring species (Laland et al., 1999; San Roman and Wagner, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Laland et al., 1999 and San Roman and Wagner, 2018

claim: The Neutral Theory of Biodiversity and Biogeography posits that all species are functionally equivalent and communities assemble via random sampling.
source: An alternative to either EC or DBD is The Neutral Theory of Biodiversity and Biogeography, in which all species are functionally equivalent and communities assemble via random sampling (Hubbell, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hubbell, 2001

claim: Neutral Theory serves as a null hypothesis of community assembly in macrobes.
source: Neutral Theory serves as a null hypothesis of community assembly in macrobes (Azaele et al., 2016; Gotelli and McGill, 2006)
evidence: Supported by citations to Azaele et al., 2016 and Gotelli and McGill, 2006

claim: Neutral Theory has been applied as a null hypothesis in microbiome research.
source: and more recently in microbiome research (Harris et al., 2017; Li and Ma, 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to Harris et al., 2017 and Li and Ma, 2016

claim: Empirical evidence for the action of EC vs. DBD in natural plant and animal communities has been mixed.
source: Empirical evidence for the action of EC vs. DBD in natural plant and animal communities has been mixed (Calcagno et al., 2017; Emerson and Kolm, 2005; Palmer and Maurer, 1997; Price et al., 2014; Rabosky et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies showing mixed results

claim: Laboratory evolution experiments tracking the diversification of a focal bacterial lineage in communities of varying complexity have yielded contradictory results, with support for EC, DBD, or intermediate scenarios.
source: Laboratory evolution experiments tracking the diversification of a focal bacterial lineage in communities of varying complexity have also yielded contradictory results, with support for EC, DBD, or intermediate scenarios (Brockhurst et al., 2007; Meyer and Kassen, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brockhurst et al., 2007 and Meyer and Kassen, 2007

claim: Diversification of a focal Pseudomonas clone was favoured by increasing community diversity in the range of 0–20 other strains or species within the same genus.
source: For example, diversification of a focal Pseudomonas clone was favoured by increasing community diversity in the range of 0–20 other strains or species within the same genus (Calcagno et al., 2017; Jousset et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to Calcagno et al., 2017 and Jousset et al., 2016

claim: Diversification was inhibited in highly diverse communities (e.g. hundreds or thousands of species in compost).
source: but diversification was inhibited in highly diverse communities (e.g. hundreds or thousands of species in compost; Gómez and Buckling, 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Gómez and Buckling, 2013

claim: Laboratory experiments are consistent with interspecific competition initially driving, but eventually inhibiting diversification as niches are filled.
source: These experiments are consistent with interspecific competition initially driving (Bailey et al., 2013), but eventually inhibiting diversification as niches are filled.
evidence: Inference from cited experiments (Bailey et al., 2013)

claim: Bacterial diversity has mostly increased over the past billion years, with speciation rates slightly exceeding extinction rates.
source: Louca et al., 2018 recently estimated that bacterial diversity has mostly increased over the past billion years, with speciation rates slightly exceeding extinction rates.
evidence: Supported by citation to Louca et al., 2018

claim: Many free-living microbes have high migration rates.
source: However, because many free-living microbes have high migration rates ('everything is everywhere, but the environment selects' [de Wit and Bouvier, 2006])
evidence: Supported by citation to de Wit and Bouvier, 2006

claim: The majority of diversity present within a typical microbiome sample is expected to be selected from a pool of migrants rather than having evolved in situ.
source: we expect that the majority of diversity present within a typical microbiome sample is selected from a pool of migrants rather than having evolved in situ
evidence: Inference based on the high migration rates of microbes

claim: The study uses 2000 microbiome samples from the Earth Microbiome Project.
source: Using high-throughput amplicon sequencing data from the Earth Microbiome Project, we provide evidence that DBD is strongest in low-diversity biomes, but weaker in more diverse biomes
evidence: Data from the Earth Microbiome Project is used in the study

claim: DBD is strongest in low-diversity biomes, but weaker in more diverse biomes.
source: Using high-throughput amplicon sequencing data from the Earth Microbiome Project, we provide evidence that DBD is strongest in low-diversity biomes, but weaker in more diverse biomes
evidence: Supported by data analysis from the Earth Microbiome Project

claim: Biotic interactions initially favour the accumulation of diversity (as predicted by DBD).
source: consistent with biotic interactions initially favouring the accumulation of diversity (as predicted by DBD)
evidence: Inference from the data analysis results

claim: As niches become increasingly filled, diversity hits a plateau (as predicted by EC).
source: However, as niches become increasingly filled, diversity hits a plateau (as predicted by EC).
evidence: Inference from the data analysis results

claim: 16S rRNA gene evolves at a rate of roughly 1–2 substitutions per million years.
source: As 16S evolves at a rate of roughly 1–2 substitutions per million years (Kuo and Ochman, 2009b)
evidence: Supported by citation to Kuo and Ochman, 2009b

claim: Evolutionary diversification within individual EMP samples cannot be uncovered using the 16S marker.
source: evolutionary diversification within individual EMP samples cannot be uncovered using this marker
evidence: Inference based on the slow evolution rate of 16S rRNA gene

claim: The EMP data represent mainly a record of community assembly.
source: rather our data represent mainly a record of community assembly
evidence: Inference from the limitations of 16S rRNA gene sequencing

claim: Generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) revealed a tendency towards positive diversity slopes with significant variation explained by the random effects of lineage, environment, and their interaction.
source: We used generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) to estimate the diversity slope at each taxonomic level in the EMP data, which revealed a tendency towards positive slopes with significant variation explained by the random effects of lineage, environment, and their interaction (Table 1, Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1–16, Supplementary file 1 Section 1).
evidence: Supported by GLMM analysis results shown in Table 1 and Figure 2

claim: All models reported provide significantly better fits compared to models without the fixed effect of community diversity.
source: All models reported here provide significantly better fits compared to models without the fixed effect of community diversity
evidence: Supported by model comparison statistics in Supplementary file 2

claim: Coefficients of determination (R2) are higher with the inclusion of random effects, showing their importance.
source: and coefficients of determination (R2) are higher with the inclusion of random effects, showing their importance (Supplementary file 2)
evidence: Supported by R2 values in Supplementary file 2

claim: Neutral Model 1 produces a significantly negative diversity slope.
source: Model 1, in which each microbiome sample is drawn from the same ZSM distribution, produces a significantly negative diversity slope (Figure 2—figure supplement 17; Table 2).
evidence: Supported by results from neutral model simulations shown in Table 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 17

claim: Neutral Model 2 slope is not significant in a GLMM accounting for variation across environments.
source: However, the Model 2 slope is not significant in a GLMM accounting for variation across environments (Table 2, Supplementary file 3 Section 1.2).
evidence: Supported by GLMM results in Table 2

claim: Most individual environments in the real EMP data tend towards a positive slope.
source: In the real EMP data, most individual environments tend towards a positive slope (Figure 2—figure supplement 18).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 18

claim: The tendency towards positive diversity slopes in the EMP is not straightforwardly explained by neutral processes.
source: The tendency towards positive diversity slopes in the EMP is therefore not straightforwardly explained by neutral processes.
evidence: Inference from comparison with neutral model results

claim: Adding DBD to null model 3 reversed the negative slope and rendered it positive.
source: As expected, adding DBD reversed the negative slope and rendered it positive (Table 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 17, Supplementary file 3 Section 2.1)
evidence: Supported by simulation results in Table 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 17

claim: The addition of EC to null model 3 had little effect on the slope, suggesting low power to detect EC under some null models.
source: In contrast, the addition of EC had little effect on the slope, suggesting low power to detect EC under some null models.
evidence: Inference from simulation results

claim: Positive diversity slopes observed in the EMP are more readily explained by DBD than by Neutral Theory.
source: Taken together, these modelling results suggest that positive diversity slopes observed in the EMP are more readily explained by DBD than by Neutral Theory
evidence: Inference from comparison of real data with neutral models and DBD/EC simulations

claim: Negative slopes could be explained by EC, Neutral Theory, or some combination of the two.
source: whereas negative slopes could be explained by EC, Neutral Theory, or some combination of the two
evidence: Inference from modeling results

claim: Nucleotide sequence-based analysis recovered generally positive diversity slopes.
source: Because taxonomic labels can be unavailable or inconsistent with phylogenetic relationships (Parks et al., 2018; Vos, 2011) we repeated the analyses using nucleotide sequence identity in the 16S rRNA gene instead of taxonomy, and again recovered generally positive diversity slopes (Materials and methods).
evidence: Supported by alternative analysis using nucleotide sequence identity

claim: GLMMs using unrarefied community Shannon diversity instead of richness obtained similar results, with generally positive diversity slopes.
source: As a final sensitivity analysis, we repeated the GLMMs using unrarefied community Shannon diversity instead of richness (Materials and methods) and obtained similar results, with generally positive diversity slopes that could in some cases be reversed depending on the lineage or environment (Table 3, Supplementary file 1 Section 2).
evidence: Supported by GLMM results using Shannon diversity shown in Table 3

claim: The Shannon diversity metric is robust to sampling effort.
source: The Shannon diversity metric is robust to sampling effort
evidence: Established knowledge about Shannon diversity

claim: Rarefaction is unlikely to bias the diversity slope downward in more diverse samples at a rarefaction to 5000 sequences.
source: Even if undersampling could bias the diversity slope downward in more diverse samples, the effect is unlikely to be large at a rarefaction to 5000 sequences, and only to occur at the extremes of diversity (e.g. very many genera and high ASV:genus ratios) and not at higher taxonomic levels (e.g. Class:Phylum) (Figure 2—figure supplement 19).
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 19

claim: A positive DBD relationship should eventually reach a plateau, giving way to EC as niches become saturated.
source: It is expected from theory and experimental studies that a positive DBD relationship should eventually reach a plateau, giving way to EC as niches become saturated (Brockhurst et al., 2007; Gómez and Buckling, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to theory and experimental studies

claim: Nucleotide sequence-based analyses support quadratic or cubic relationships over linear diversity slopes.
source: This expectation is borne out in our dataset, particularly in the nucleotide sequence-based analyses which support quadratic or cubic relationships over linear diversity slopes (Figure 2—figure supplement 20).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 20

claim: In the animal distal gut, a relatively low-diversity biome, a strong linear DBD relationship was observed at most phylogenetic depths.
source: For example, in the animal distal gut, a relatively low-diversity biome, we observed a strong linear DBD relationship at most phylogenetic depths
evidence: Supported by data analysis of animal distal gut samples

claim: The much more diverse soil biome clearly reaches a plateau in the DBD relationship.
source: in contrast, the much more diverse soil biome clearly reaches a plateau (Figure 2—figure supplements 21–26)
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 21–26

claim: Diversity slopes were significantly higher in less diverse (often host-associated) biomes.
source: Diversity slopes were significantly higher in less diverse (often host-associated) biomes, suggesting that niche filling leads to a plateau of DBD in more diverse biomes (Figure 3, Supplementary file 1 Section 3).
evidence: Supported by GLMM results shown in Figure 3

claim: The interaction observed in the real EMP data between community diversity and biome type in shaping focal lineage diversity was not observed under a neutral null (Model 2).
source: The interaction observed in the real EMP data between community diversity and biome type in shaping focal lineage diversity was not observed under a neutral null (Model 2, in which each environment has its own characteristic level of diversity) (Supplementary file 3 Section 1.2).
evidence: Supported by comparison with neutral model results

claim: The DBD plateau observed in more diverse biomes is not readily explained by a neutral model.
source: The DBD plateau observed in more diverse biomes is thus not readily explained by a neutral model
evidence: Inference from comparison with neutral model results

claim: Rarefaction is not expected to bias the diversity slope estimates, particularly at the Class:Phylum level.
source: nor is rarefaction expected to bias the diversity slope estimates, particularly at the Class:Phylum level (Figure 2—figure supplement 19)
evidence: Supported by simulation results in Figure 2—figure supplement 19

claim: The plateau of DBD at higher levels of community diversity is not an artefact of data structure or sampling effort.
source: This suggests that the plateau of DBD at higher levels of community diversity is not an artefact of data structure or sampling effort.
evidence: Inference from rarefaction simulation results

claim: Cell density is unlikely to drive the trend of decreasing diversity slopes with increasing community diversity.
source: It is clear from this figure that relatively high- and low-density samples are found along the range of community taxonomic diversities, demonstrating that cell density is unlikely to drive the trend of decreasing diversity slopes with increasing community diversity.
evidence: Inference from comparison of cell density estimates with diversity slopes shown in Figure 3

claim: Community diversity generally had significant positive effects on focal-lineage diversity in the EMP subset with abiotic measurements.
source: As in the full EMP dataset (Table 1), focal lineage diversity was positively associated with community diversity at all taxonomic ratios in the EMP subset (Table 4).
evidence: Supported by GLMM results in Table 4

claim: Certain abiotic factors, alone or in combination with diversity, had significant effects on focal lineage diversity.
source: As expected, certain abiotic factors, alone or in combination with diversity, had significant effects on focal lineage diversity (Table 4).
evidence: Supported by GLMM results in Table 4

claim: The effects of abiotic factors were always weaker than the effect of community diversity in the EMP subset.
source: However, the effects of abiotic factors were always weaker than the effect of community diversity (Table 4; Supplementary file 1 Section 4).
evidence: Supported by comparison of effect sizes in Table 4

claim: In the soil dataset, community diversity generally had significant positive effects on focal-lineage diversity, but the effect was weak and not detectable at all taxonomic ratios.
source: Community diversity generally had significant positive effects on focal-lineage diversity, but the effect was weak and not detectable at all taxonomic ratios (Table 5).
evidence: Supported by GLMM results in Table 5

claim: Known abiotic drivers of soil bacterial diversity such as pH and latitude had effects of similar or stronger magnitude compared to the effect of community diversity in the soil dataset.
source: Known abiotic drivers of soil bacterial diversity such as pH (Lauber et al., 2009) and latitude (Delgado-Baquerizo et al., 2018) had effects of similar or stronger magnitude compared to the effect of community diversity (Table 5, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Supported by GLMM results in Table 5 and citations to studies on pH and latitude effects

claim: The relatively weak effect of DBD and strong effect of abiotic drivers on diversity in the soil dataset can be explained by the fact that soils generally are highly diverse and have relatively low-diversity slopes.
source: The relatively weak effect of DBD and strong effect of abiotic drivers on diversity in this soil dataset can be explained by the fact that soils generally are highly diverse and have relatively low-diversity slopes (Figure 3).
evidence: Inference from comparison of soil results with Figure 3

claim: Resident community diversity had no significant effect on the diversity of generalists in animal-associated, saline and non-saline clusters.
source: Resident community diversity had no significant effect on the diversity of generalists in animal-associated, saline and non-saline clusters (GLMM, Wald test, p>0.05)
evidence: Supported by GLMM results

claim: Resident community diversity was positively correlated with lineage-specific resident diversity in all three environment clusters.
source: but was positively correlated with lineage-specific resident diversity (GLMM, Wald test, z = 7.1, p=1.25e-12; z = 3.316, p=0.0009; z = 7.109, p=1.17e-12, respectively)
evidence: Supported by GLMM results with specific test statistics

claim: Resident community diversity significantly decreased migrant diversity in saline and non-saline environment clusters.
source: Resident community diversity significantly decreased migrant diversity in saline (GLMM, z = −3.194, p=0.0014) and non-saline environment clusters (GLMM, z = −2.840, p=0.0045)
evidence: Supported by GLMM results with specific test statistics

claim: Resident community diversity had no significant effect on migrant diversity in the animal-associated cluster.
source: but had no significant effect in the animal-associated cluster (GLMM, p>0.05) (Figure 4b)
evidence: Supported by GLMM results shown in Figure 4b

claim: Generalist lineages have lower diversity slopes than resident lineages.
source: These results suggest that, although generalist lineages may have higher speciation rates and colonize more habitats than specialists (Sriswasdi et al., 2017), they have lower diversity slopes.
evidence: Inference from GLMM results and citation to Sriswasdi et al., 2017

claim: Migrants to the 'wrong' environment experience even less DBD, and are even subject to EC in two out of three environment types.
source: Migrants to the 'wrong' environment experience even less DBD, and are even subject to EC in two out of three environment types (Figure 4b).
evidence: Supported by results shown in Figure 4b

claim: The accumulation of diversity via successful establishment of migrants may be limited because most niches are already occupied by residents.
source: The accumulation of diversity via successful establishment of migrants may thus be limited, presumably because most niches are already occupied by residents.
evidence: Inference from the results on resident vs. migrant diversity

claim: There is an overall trend for diversity in focal lineages to be positively associated with overall community diversity, albeit with significant variation across lineages and environments.
source: Using ~10 million individual marker sequences from the EMP, we demonstrate an overall trend for diversity in focal lineages to be positively associated with overall community diversity, albeit with significant variation across lineages and environments.
evidence: Supported by data analysis of EMP sequences

claim: The strength of the DBD relationship dissipates with increasing microbiome diversity, which is hypothesized to be caused by niche saturation.
source: The strength of the DBD relationship dissipates with increasing microbiome diversity, which we hypothesize is caused by niche saturation.
evidence: Inference from data analysis results

claim: In more diverse biomes such as soil, abiotic factors may become relatively more important in driving focal-lineage diversity.
source: In more diverse biomes such as soil, abiotic factors therefore may become relatively more important in driving focal-lineage diversity.
evidence: Inference from comparison of EMP and soil dataset results

claim: The effect of DBD is strongest among habitat specialists (residents).
source: The effect of DBD is strongest among habitat specialists (residents)
evidence: Supported by analysis of resident vs. generalist diversity

claim: Long-term niche adaptation tends to select against the establishment of migrant diversity.
source: suggesting that long-term niche adaptation tends to select against the establishment of migrant diversity
evidence: Inference from results on resident vs. migrant diversity

claim: At the limited resolution of 16S rRNA gene sequences, measurable diversification within an individual microbiome sample is not expected.
source: At the limited resolution of 16S rRNA gene sequences, we do not expect measurable diversification within an individual microbiome sample (Kuo and Ochman, 2009b)
evidence: Based on knowledge of 16S rRNA gene evolution rate cited from Kuo and Ochman, 2009b

claim: Community diversity could still select for or against increasing diversity in a focal lineage, even if this lineage diversified before the sampled community assembled.
source: however, community diversity could still select for (as in DBD) or against (as in EC) increasing diversity in a focal lineage, even if this lineage diversified before the sampled community assembled
evidence: Inference about community assembly processes

claim: Bacteria with larger repertoires of accessory genes, and thus larger genomes, are able to occupy a wider range of niches.
source: Bacteria with larger repertoires of accessory genes, and thus larger genomes, are able to occupy a wider range of niches (Barberán et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Barberán et al., 2014

claim: There is a significant positive effect of genome size on the diversity slope.
source: Consistent with our expectation, we observed a significant positive effect of genome size on the diversity slope (GLMM, Wald test, z = 2.5, p=0.01; Figure 5, Supplementary file 1 Section 6).
evidence: Supported by GLMM results shown in Figure 5

claim: The effect of genome size on diversity slope was not observed in null models.
source: This effect was not observed in null models, in which the interaction between community diversity and focal genus genome size was never significant (Supplementary file 3 Section 1.3 and 2.2)
evidence: Supported by null model results

claim: The effect of genome size on DBD cannot be trivially explained by data structure.
source: and so this effect of genome size cannot be trivially explained by data structure
evidence: Inference from comparison with null models

claim: The positive relationship between genome size and DBD is likely even stronger than estimated, because assigning genome sizes to entire genera is imprecise.
source: The positive relationship between genome size and DBD is likely even stronger than estimated, because assigning genome sizes to entire genera is imprecise (i.e. there is variation in genome size within a genus, or even within species), therefore weakening the correlation.
evidence: Inference about measurement error

claim: The positive correlation between genome size and DBD could be driven by larger metabolic repertoires encoded by larger genomes, potentially creating more opportunities to benefit from cross-feeding, niche construction, and other interspecies interactions.
source: The positive correlation between genome size and DBD observed here could be driven by larger metabolic repertoires encoded by larger genomes (Barberán et al., 2014), potentially creating more opportunities to benefit from cross-feeding, niche construction (San Roman and Wagner, 2018), and other interspecies interactions.
evidence: Speculation based on citations to Barberán et al., 2014 and San Roman and Wagner, 2018

claim: The Black Queen hypothesis predicts that social conflict between interacting species leads to the inactivation and loss of genes involved in shareable metabolites, eventually resulting in reduced genome size.
source: This tendency appears to be at odds with the Black Queen hypothesis, which predicts that social conflict between interacting species leads to the inactivation and loss of genes involved in shareable metabolites (public goods), eventually resulting in reduced genome size (Morris et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Morris et al., 2012

claim: The Black Queen hypothesis would produce a negative correlation between the degree of species interactions (i.e. community diversity) and genome size.
source: Such a process would produce a negative correlation between the degree of species interactions (i.e. community diversity) and genome size (Morris et al., 2012).
evidence: Inference from the Black Queen hypothesis cited from Morris et al., 2012

claim: The EMP survey data provide a window into the biotic drivers of microbial diversity in nature.
source: Alongside theory and experimental data, the EMP survey data provide a window into the biotic drivers of microbial diversity in nature.
evidence: Inference about the contribution of the study

claim: The correlational results support previous experiments and theory showing that DBD is strong when community diversity is low.
source: In particular, our correlational results support previous experiments and theory showing that DBD is strong when community diversity is low (Calcagno et al., 2017; Jousset et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by comparison with cited experiments and theory

claim: DBD drives the accumulation of diversity in a positive feedback loop until niches are filled and EC starts to predominate.
source: driving the accumulation of diversity in a positive feedback loop until niches are filled and EC starts to predominate (Bailey et al., 2013; Brockhurst et al., 2007; Gómez and Buckling, 2013; Meyer and Kassen, 2007)
evidence: Inference supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Due to the correlational nature of the EMP data, it is not possible to test whether DBD is primarily due to the creation of novel niches via biotic interactions and niche construction, or due to increased competition leading to specialization on underexploited resources.
source: However, due to the correlational nature of the EMP data, it is not possible to test whether DBD is primarily due to the creation of novel niches via biotic interactions and niche construction (Laland et al., 1999), or due to increased competition leading to specialization on underexploited resources (Hibbing et al., 2010; Jousset et al., 2016).
evidence: Acknowledgment of study limitations with citations to relevant mechanisms

claim: The results demonstrate a general scaling between different levels of community diversity, which has important implications for modelling and predicting community function and stability in response to perturbations.
source: Regardless of the underlying mechanisms, our results demonstrate a general scaling between different levels of community diversity, which has important implications for modelling and predicting community function and stability in response to perturbations (Coyte et al., 2015; Pennekamp et al., 2018).
evidence: Inference about implications of the results, with citations to relevant studies

claim: All samples were rarefied to 5000 observations to avoid a trivially positive diversity slope due to variation in sequencing effort.
source: To avoid a trivially positive diversity slope due to variation in sequencing effort, all samples were rarefied to 5000 observations (counts of 16S rRNA gene sequences), as diversity estimates are highly sensitive to sampling effort (Gotelli and Colwell, 2001).
evidence: Methodological choice supported by citation to Gotelli and Colwell, 2001

claim: The EMP '2000 subset' contains 155,002 ASVs from 2000 samples with an even distribution across 17 natural environments.
source: We used the EMP '2000 subset' of 16S rRNA gene sequences, rarefied to 5000 sequences per sample. This subset contains 155,002 ASVs from 2000 samples with an even distribution across 17 natural environments (EMP Ontology level 3).
evidence: Description of the dataset used
